concept.name: London 4 p.m. fix
concept.definition: The daily reference exchange rate computed from market activity in a window around 4:00 p.m. London time, historically administered as the WM/Reuters benchmark. It is the most widely used FX fixing for valuing funds, settling derivatives and executing customer orders, and was the focus of the 2013-15 benchmark-manipulation investigations and the subsequent 2015 reform that widened the fixing window.
concept.intuition: The 4 p.m. London fix is the FX market's global 'closing price' — the single rate the world's asset managers use to value and convert currencies.
concept.mechanics: The rate is computed from actual trades and order data over a window centred on 4 p.m. London time; the window was lengthened from one minute to five minutes in the 2015 reform to reduce manipulability. Banks accepting client fix orders guarantee execution at the fix price and hedge the resulting exposure, which produces volume spikes and characteristic price dynamics in the window — patterns that persisted in altered form after the reform, as banks shifted to passive execution strategies.
concept.failure_modes: The pre-2015 one-minute window was manipulable: traders at major banks colluded to push the fix, resulting in multi-billion-dollar fines. Post-reform, the fix still exhibits anomalous price dynamics and heavy month-end volume, so execution quality at the fix can differ systematically from prevailing market prices.
concept.misconceptions: The fix is not set in London by a committee of quotes (like old LIBOR) — it is computed from actual market transaction data in the window — and trading 'at the fix' does not guarantee the mid-market price.
concept.example: A global equity fund's NAV converts its foreign holdings to dollars each day using the WM/Reuters 4 p.m. rates, so its reported performance is tied to those fix prints.

citations.source: NBER Working Paper 23327 — Did the Reform Fix the London Fix Problem? (Ito and Yamada)
